newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition urges more protests over polls.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition urges more protests over polls.

text.p: Serbian opposition leaders urged their followers to keep up the pressure on authorities to recognise their victory in local elections, amid signs that their wave of street demonstrations was running out of steam.

The opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition appealed to supporters to protest on Thursday in the capital Belgrade against the ruling Socialists, accusing the authorities of committing extensive fraud to annul the results.
The coalition organised demonstrations in Belgrade and several major towns on Wednesday but Socialist authorities showed no sign they were ready to bow to popular protest.

The demonstrations, held under a light rain, attracted thousands of people but the crowds were smaller than the previous day. Organisers appeared hesitant to provoke a violent clash with a heavily-armed police force.
Electoral officials on Tuesday confirmed the opposition's victory in the capital Belgrade, an unprecedented defeat for the Socialists led by President Slobodan Milosevic.
But authorities failed to confirm opposition victories in other towns where Zajedno said it also scored clear majorities.
Electoral commissions controlled by the Socialists have cited unspecified irregularities in municipalities where the opposition said it won majorities, and ordered another round of voting.
The three leaders of the coalition and other opposition members of parliament went on hunger strike in Belgrade on Wednesday evening, demanding authorities verify the results.
The 66 opposition representatives said they would stay inside the Serbian parliament "until the democratically expressed desires of the people are fulfilled".
From the fifth floor window, Vuk Draskovic, one of the Zajedno leaders, addressed a crowd of 2,000 that gathered outside the building.

"I appeal to all of you to defend our electoral will, to go out into the streets and by your numbers, your strength and the perseverance you will show over the coming days, force the people who organised this completely unprecedented election fraud to see reason," said Draskovic, his voice hoarse.

He read a letter to Milosevic calling on the former communist party chief to abide by the country's constitution. Draskovic led street demonstrations for press freedom in 1991 which Milosevic crushed with the police and the army.
The opposition coalition appealed to the United States and the European Union to support their protests, Draskovic said.
Western powers, however, view Milosevic as crucial for the implementation of the peace treaty that ended the Bosnian war last year.
Draskovic called the West's attitude "shameful" and told reporters a democratically-elected opposition would be more capable of bringing real peace to the Balkans.
"New people who were from the beginning...against ethnic cleansing and war crimes can establish a stable peace, reconciliation and repentance in the Balkans," he said.
Socialist authorities bused in police with riot gear to protect town halls in several towns but no clashes had been reported early on Thursday.
A leftist coalition including the Socialists prevailed in federal elections held earlier this month after a state media campaign which portrayed Milosevic as a peacemaker.
But in the run-off for municipal elections held on Sunday, the Socialists suffered a humiliating defeat in the country's major industrial centres.
Although it was an unprecedented setback for Milosevic, he retains supreme authority in a country which human rights workers describe as an authoritarian police state.

Milosevic has ruled Serbia with an iron fist since he first rose to prominence by whipping up Serb nationalist fervour. He has since purged nationalist hardliners in his party and recast himself as a guarantor of stability in the Balkans.
Barring a sustained, massive popular protest, political analysts said the Socialists -- backed by the police and the state media -- were likely to succeed in cancelling the opposition's victories.
